claim: Individual neurons of the brain can display somatic genomic mosaicism of unknown function.
source: Previous reports have shown that individual neurons of the brain can display somatic genomic mosaicism of unknown function.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature, as indicated by the reference to 'previous reports'.

claim: Sporadic Alzheimer's disease neurons display altered genomic mosaicism characterized by increases in DNA content.
source: In this study, we report altered genomic mosaicism in single, sporadic Alzheimer's disease (AD) neurons characterized by increases in DNA content and amyloid precursor protein (APP) gene copy number.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Sporadic Alzheimer's disease neurons display altered genomic mosaicism characterized by increases in amyloid precursor protein (APP) gene copy number.
source: In this study, we report altered genomic mosaicism in single, sporadic Alzheimer's disease (AD) neurons characterized by increases in DNA content and amyloid precursor protein (APP) gene copy number.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: AD cortical nuclei displayed average DNA content increases of approximately 8% over non-diseased controls.
source: AD cortical nuclei displayed large variability with average DNA content increases of ∼8% over non-diseased controls that were unrelated to trisomy 21.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from DNA content analysis experiments presented in the study.

claim: The DNA content increases in AD cortical nuclei were unrelated to trisomy 21.
source: AD cortical nuclei displayed large variability with average DNA content increases of ∼8% over non-diseased controls that were unrelated to trisomy 21.
evidence: This is supported by FISH analysis data presented in the study showing no significant differences in trisomy 21 rates.

claim: Two independent single-cell copy number analyses identified amplifications at the APP locus.
source: Two independent single-cell copy number analyses identified amplifications at the APP locus.
evidence: This refers to experimental data from single-cell qPCR and PNA-FISH analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: Single-cell qPCR identified up to 12 copies of APP in sampled neurons.
source: The use of single-cell qPCR identified up to 12 copies of APP in sampled neurons.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from single-cell qPCR experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Peptide nucleic acid (PNA) probes targeting APP, combined with super-resolution microscopy, detected primarily single fluorescent signals of variable intensity that paralleled single-cell qPCR analyses.
source: Peptide nucleic acid (PNA) probes targeting APP, combined with super-resolution microscopy detected primarily single fluorescent signals of variable intensity that paralleled single-cell qPCR analyses.
evidence: This is supported by PNA-FISH experimental data presented in Figure 7.

claim: Somatic genomic changes in single neurons affect known and unknown loci and are increased in sporadic AD.
source: These data identify somatic genomic changes in single neurons, affecting known and unknown loci, which are increased in sporadic AD, and further indicate functionality for genomic mosaicism in the CNS.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the experimental data showing DNA content increases and APP copy number variations.

claim: Genomic mosaicism has functionality in the CNS.
source: These data identify somatic genomic changes in single neurons, affecting known and unknown loci, which are increased in sporadic AD, and further indicate functionality for genomic mosaicism in the CNS.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the association between genomic mosaicism and disease state.

claim: Somatic genomic mosaicism in neurons includes aneuploidy.
source: Identified forms of somatically arising genomic mosaicism include aneuploidy (reviewed in Bushman and Chun, 2013), LINE elements (Muotri et al., 2005; Baillie et al., 2011; Evrony et al., 2012), copy number variations (CNVs) (Gole et al., 2013; McConnell et al., 2013; Cai et al., 2014), and DNA content variation (DCV) (Westra et al., 2010; Fischer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Somatic genomic mosaicism in neurons includes LINE elements.
source: Identified forms of somatically arising genomic mosaicism include aneuploidy (reviewed in Bushman and Chun, 2013), LINE elements (Muotri et al., 2005; Baillie et al., 2011; Evrony et al., 2012), copy number variations (CNVs) (Gole et al., 2013; McConnell et al., 2013; Cai et al., 2014), and DNA content variation (DCV) (Westra et al., 2010; Fischer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Muotri et al., 2005; Baillie et al., 2011; Evrony et al., 2012).

claim: Somatic genomic mosaicism in neurons includes copy number variations (CNVs).
source: Identified forms of somatically arising genomic mosaicism include aneuploidy (reviewed in Bushman and Chun, 2013), LINE elements (Muotri et al., 2005; Baillie et al., 2011; Evrony et al., 2012), copy number variations (CNVs) (Gole et al., 2013; McConnell et al., 2013; Cai et al., 2014), and DNA content variation (DCV) (Westra et al., 2010; Fischer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Gole et al., 2013; McConnell et al., 2013; Cai et al., 2014).

claim: Somatic genomic mosaicism in neurons includes DNA content variation (DCV).
source: Identified forms of somatically arising genomic mosaicism include aneuploidy (reviewed in Bushman and Chun, 2013), LINE elements (Muotri et al., 2005; Baillie et al., 2011; Evrony et al., 2012), copy number variations (CNVs) (Gole et al., 2013; McConnell et al., 2013; Cai et al., 2014), and DNA content variation (DCV) (Westra et al., 2010; Fischer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Westra et al., 2010; Fischer et al., 2012).

claim: AD is the most common form of dementia.
source: AD is the most common form of dementia and is characterized by the presence of amyloid plaques, synaptic loss, and cell death (Alzheimer's Association, 2013), notably affecting the prefrontal cortex.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Alzheimer's Association, 2013.

claim: AD is characterized by the presence of amyloid plaques, synaptic loss, and cell death.
source: AD is the most common form of dementia and is characterized by the presence of amyloid plaques, synaptic loss, and cell death (Alzheimer's Association, 2013), notably affecting the prefrontal cortex.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Alzheimer's Association, 2013.

claim: AD notably affects the prefrontal cortex.
source: AD is the most common form of dementia and is characterized by the presence of amyloid plaques, synaptic loss, and cell death (Alzheimer's Association, 2013), notably affecting the prefrontal cortex.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: β-amyloid (Aβ) is the major component of amyloid plaques.
source: The major component of these plaques is β-amyloid (Aβ), a protein encoded by APP (Goldgaber et al., 1987; St George-Hyslop et al., 1987; Tanzi et al., 1987).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to foundational literature (Goldgaber et al., 1987; St George-Hyslop et al., 1987; Tanzi et al., 1987).

claim: β-amyloid (Aβ) is encoded by APP.
source: The major component of these plaques is β-amyloid (Aβ), a protein encoded by APP (Goldgaber et al., 1987; St George-Hyslop et al., 1987; Tanzi et al., 1987).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to foundational literature (Goldgaber et al., 1987; St George-Hyslop et al., 1987; Tanzi et al., 1987).

claim: Familial AD accounts for less than 5% of all AD cases.
source: Familial AD accounts for less than 5% of all cases and has been genetically linked to mutations in APP and two presenilins (PSEN), PSEN1 and PSEN2, the catalytic components of γ-secretase and the units responsible for cleavage of APP (Price and Sisodia, 1998; Bertram et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Familial AD has been genetically linked to mutations in APP.
source: Familial AD accounts for less than 5% of all cases and has been genetically linked to mutations in APP and two presenilins (PSEN), PSEN1 and PSEN2, the catalytic components of γ-secretase and the units responsible for cleavage of APP (Price and Sisodia, 1998; Bertram et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations (Price and Sisodia, 1998; Bertram et al., 2010).

claim: Familial AD has been genetically linked to mutations in PSEN1 and PSEN2.
source: Familial AD accounts for less than 5% of all cases and has been genetically linked to mutations in APP and two presenilins (PSEN), PSEN1 and PSEN2, the catalytic components of γ-secretase and the units responsible for cleavage of APP (Price and Sisodia, 1998; Bertram et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations (Price and Sisodia, 1998; Bertram et al., 2010).

claim: PSEN1 and PSEN2 are the catalytic components of γ-secretase.
source: Familial AD accounts for less than 5% of all cases and has been genetically linked to mutations in APP and two presenilins (PSEN), PSEN1 and PSEN2, the catalytic components of γ-secretase and the units responsible for cleavage of APP (Price and Sisodia, 1998; Bertram et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations (Price and Sisodia, 1998; Bertram et al., 2010).

claim: PSEN1 and PSEN2 are responsible for cleavage of APP.
source: Familial AD accounts for less than 5% of all cases and has been genetically linked to mutations in APP and two presenilins (PSEN), PSEN1 and PSEN2, the catalytic components of γ-secretase and the units responsible for cleavage of APP (Price and Sisodia, 1998; Bertram et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations (Price and Sisodia, 1998; Bertram et al., 2010).

claim: APP gene dosage is strongly associated with AD pathogenesis.
source: In addition, APP gene dosage is strongly associated with AD pathogenesis based on multiple lines of evidence.
evidence: This is supported by multiple lines of evidence cited in the manuscript including Down syndrome and familial AD studies.

claim: Down syndrome, with three copies of APP, produces neuropathology virtually identical to AD.
source: First, Down syndrome (DS), with three copies of APP, produces neuropathology virtually identical to AD (Glenner and Wong, 1984; Delabar et al., 1987) and APP locus duplications are sufficient to cause familial AD (Rovelet-Lecrux et al., 2006; Sleegers et al., 2006; McNaughton et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations (Glenner and Wong, 1984; Delabar et al., 1987).

claim: APP locus duplications are sufficient to cause familial AD.
source: First, Down syndrome (DS), with three copies of APP, produces neuropathology virtually identical to AD (Glenner and Wong, 1984; Delabar et al., 1987) and APP locus duplications are sufficient to cause familial AD (Rovelet-Lecrux et al., 2006; Sleegers et al., 2006; McNaughton et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations (Rovelet-Lecrux et al., 2006; Sleegers et al., 2006; McNaughton et al., 2012).

claim: AD-protective effects have been reported in DS with APP deletion via partial trisomy.
source: Moreover, AD-protective effects have been reported in DS with APP deletion via partial trisomy (Prasher et al., 1998), as well as in familial AD with an APP partial loss-of-function mutation (Jonsson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Prasher et al., 1998.

claim: AD-protective effects have been reported in familial AD with an APP partial loss-of-function mutation.
source: Moreover, AD-protective effects have been reported in DS with APP deletion via partial trisomy (Prasher et al., 1998), as well as in familial AD with an APP partial loss-of-function mutation (Jonsson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jonsson et al., 2012.

claim: Seminal studies in the 1980s failed to detect evidence of APP amplification in sporadic Alzheimer's disease peripheral blood and whole brain.
source: However, seminal studies in the 1980s failed to detect evidence of APP amplification in sporadic Alzheimer's disease peripheral blood and whole brain (Podlisny et al., 1987; St George-Hyslop et al., 1987; Tanzi et al., 1987) despite strong linkage in familial AD, thus linkage between sporadic AD and APP remains unclear.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Podlisny et al., 1987; St George-Hyslop et al., 1987; Tanzi et al., 1987).

claim: Linkage between sporadic AD and APP remains unclear.
source: However, seminal studies in the 1980s failed to detect evidence of APP amplification in sporadic Alzheimer's disease peripheral blood and whole brain (Podlisny et al., 1987; St George-Hyslop et al., 1987; Tanzi et al., 1987) despite strong linkage in familial AD, thus linkage between sporadic AD and APP remains unclear.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of prior evidence for APP amplification in sporadic AD despite strong linkage in familial AD.

claim: Region specific genomic mosaicism exists in the normal brain.
source: The existence of region specific genomic mosaicism in the normal brain (Westra et al., 2010) raised the possibility that DCV, defined as variations in the total DNA amount present in a single cell or population, might play a functional role in sporadic brain diseases by altering pathogenic loci in individual cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Westra et al., 2010.

claim: DCV is defined as variations in the total DNA amount present in a single cell or population.
source: The existence of region specific genomic mosaicism in the normal brain (Westra et al., 2010) raised the possibility that DCV, defined as variations in the total DNA amount present in a single cell or population, might play a functional role in sporadic brain diseases by altering pathogenic loci in individual cells.
evidence: This is a definition provided in the text.

claim: DCV might play a functional role in sporadic brain diseases by altering pathogenic loci in individual cells.
source: The existence of region specific genomic mosaicism in the normal brain (Westra et al., 2010) raised the possibility that DCV, defined as variations in the total DNA amount present in a single cell or population, might play a functional role in sporadic brain diseases by altering pathogenic loci in individual cells.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on prior observations and the current study's rationale.

claim: Mosaic alterations in APP copy number within single neurons may play a role in producing sporadic AD.
source: The validated pathogenicity of APP in familial AD suggested that mosaic alterations in APP copy number within single neurons may play a role in producing sporadic AD.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the pathogenicity of APP in familial AD and the possibility of mosaic changes.

claim: Five independent experimental approaches were used to report increased somatic genomic variation within individual sporadic AD neurons.
source: Through the use of five independent experimental approaches, we report increased somatic genomic variation within individual sporadic AD neurons involving mosaic increases in both DNA content and APP copy number.
evidence: This refers to the experimental design and data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Increased somatic genomic variation in sporadic AD neurons involves mosaic increases in both DNA content and APP copy number.
source: Through the use of five independent experimental approaches, we report increased somatic genomic variation within individual sporadic AD neurons involving mosaic increases in both DNA content and APP copy number.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Neuronal nuclei were isolated from paired prefrontal cortex and cerebellum of postmortem human brains.
source: First, neuronal nuclei were isolated from paired prefrontal cortex and cerebellum of postmortem human brains as previously described (Figure 1A) (Westra et al., 2008, 2010).
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology shown in Figure 1A and references prior methods (Westra et al., 2008, 2010).

claim: PI staining intensity faithfully reports DNA content.
source: In every case, nuclei with high PI intensity also showed increased DNA synthesis over those with low PI intensity. These results independently confirm, as expected, that PI staining intensity faithfully reports DNA content.
evidence: This is validated by whole genome amplification experiments shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Nuclei with high PI intensity showed increased DNA synthesis over those with low PI intensity.
source: In every case, nuclei with high PI intensity also showed increased DNA synthesis over those with low PI intensity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the WGA validation experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: AD cerebellar nuclei showed DNA content profiles similar to lymphocytes.
source: In control experiments, AD cerebellar nuclei showed DNA content profiles similar to lymphocytes, characterized by histograms with sharp peaks and narrow bases (Figure 2C,E).
evidence: This is shown in the DNA content histograms in Figure 2C and 2E.

claim: AD cortices displayed high variability characterized by right hand shoulders, large right hand peak shifts, and wide bases.
source: By comparison, AD cortices displayed high variability characterized by right hand shoulders (Figure 2D,E [AD-7]), large right hand peak shifts (Figure 2D,E [AD-6]), and wide bases.
evidence: This is shown in the DNA content histograms in Figure 2D and 2E.

claim: Greater than 90% of AD cortex samples examined displayed a net DNA content increase.
source: Of the AD cortex samples examined, greater than 90% displayed a net DNA content increase, averaging approximately 8% gain over human lymphocyte controls (Figure 2F–H).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from DNA content analysis shown in Figure 2F-H.

claim: The AD cortex displayed increases beyond those observed in non-diseased cortices, with an average gain of approximately 6% over age and sex-matched samples.
source: Notably, the AD cortex displayed increases beyond those observed in non-diseased cortices, with an average gain of approximately 6% over age and sex-matched samples (Figure 2F–H).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from DNA content analysis shown in Figure 2F-H.

claim: AD cortices displayed an increased coefficient of variation over non-diseased cortical nuclei and all cerebellar nuclei.
source: AD cortices also displayed an increased coefficient of variation over non-diseased cortical nuclei and all cerebellar nuclei (Figure 2I) as well as a consistent skewed distribution compared to AD cerebellum (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2I and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: AD cortices displayed a consistent skewed distribution compared to AD cerebellum.
source: AD cortices also displayed an increased coefficient of variation over non-diseased cortical nuclei and all cerebellar nuclei (Figure 2I) as well as a consistent skewed distribution compared to AD cerebellum (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In AD and non-diseased brain samples, DNA content changes did not correlate with age, Braak score, or postmortem index.
source: In addition, we examined 14 paired sets of AD cortex and cerebellum from the same individual (Figure 3A) and 12 paired sets from non-diseased individuals (Figure 3B). Each AD cortex showed unique cortical histograms and increases in total cortical DNA compared to the cerebellum. In AD and non-diseased brain samples, DNA content changes did not correlate with age, Braak score, or postmortem index (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–H), and DNA content was independent of nuclear size (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) (Westra et al., 2010).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B-H.

claim: DNA content was independent of nuclear size.
source: In AD and non-diseased brain samples, DNA content changes did not correlate with age, Braak score, or postmortem index (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–H), and DNA content was independent of nuclear size (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) (Westra et al., 2010).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and supported by citation to Westra et al., 2010.

claim: The DNA content increase observed was significantly less than a 4N tetraploid genome.
source: Importantly, the increase observed was significantly less than a 4N tetraploid genome (∼12,800 Mb), yet significantly more than what would be expected from a hypersomy of even the largest chromosome (chr1: ∼250 Mb or 3.9%).
evidence: This is an inference based on the quantitative DNA content measurements and known genome sizes.

claim: The DNA content increase observed was significantly more than what would be expected from a hypersomy of even the largest chromosome.
source: Importantly, the increase observed was significantly less than a 4N tetraploid genome (∼12,800 Mb), yet significantly more than what would be expected from a hypersomy of even the largest chromosome (chr1: ∼250 Mb or 3.9%).
evidence: This is an inference based on the quantitative DNA content measurements and known chromosome sizes.

claim: Neuroanatomically selective increases in DNA content represent a distinct, reproducible, and prevalent characteristic of the AD brain.
source: These results indicate that neuroanatomically selective increases in DNA content represent a distinct, reproducible, and prevalent characteristic of the AD brain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the DNA content analysis data showing consistent increases in AD cortex.

claim: In the non-diseased cortex, neurons were identified as the predominant cell type contributing to increased DCV.
source: In the non-diseased cortex, neurons were identified as the predominant cell type contributing to increased DCV (Westra et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Westra et al., 2010.

claim: NeuN-positive AD cortical neurons showed right hand DNA content shifts.
source: NeuN-positive AD cortical neurons showed right hand DNA content shifts (Figure 4D) and increased DCV, displaying ∼9% gain over that observed in NeuN-negative nuclei (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D and 4E from NeuN immunolabeling and flow cytometry experiments.

claim: NeuN-positive AD cortical neurons displayed approximately 9% gain in DNA content over NeuN-negative nuclei.
source: NeuN-positive AD cortical neurons showed right hand DNA content shifts (Figure 4D) and increased DCV, displaying ∼9% gain over that observed in NeuN-negative nuclei (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding shown in Figure 4E.

claim: NeuN-positive nuclei in paired samples from the same brain showed significantly increased DNA content in cortical neurons over cerebellar neurons.
source: A comparison of NeuN-positive nuclei in paired samples from the same brain also showed significantly increased DNA content in cortical neurons over cerebellar neurons (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4F from paired sample analysis.

claim: Neurons are the major cellular locus for increased DCV in AD.
source: These distinctions do not rule out AD-specific effects on DCV from non-neuronal cells, but do implicate neurons as the major cellular locus for increased DCV.
evidence: This is an inference based on the NeuN-positive cell analysis showing neurons have the greatest DNA content increases.

claim: Three of six AD samples displayed significant increases in APP copy number over paired cerebellar samples.
source: Three of six AD samples displayed significant increases in APP copy number (3.9–6.3 copies compared to reference genes) over paired cerebellar samples (Figure 5A (AD-1, AD-3, AD-6)).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A from small population qPCR experiments.

claim: Similar APP amplification was not detected in non-diseased brains.
source: Similar APP amplification was not detected in non-diseased brains (Figure 5B), and DS controls along with reference gene assessments demonstrated expected results (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B from small population qPCR experiments.

claim: AD samples displayed substantial variability in APP copies.
source: Notably, AD samples displayed substantial variability in APP copies (Figure 5C), revealing inherent limitations in precisely quantifying copy numbers in small, genomically mosaic cell populations and highlighting the necessity for single-cell analyses.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C and represents an observation from the qPCR data.

claim: No statistically significant changes in chromosome 21 aneuploidy rates, including trisomies, between AD and non-diseased brains were observed.
source: Despite using liberal counting criteria, no statistically significant changes in chromosome 21 aneuploidy rates, including trisomies, between AD (N = 4974 nuclei, N = 9 brains) and non-diseased brains (N = 2576 nuclei, N = 5 brains) were observed (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5J from FISH analysis of chromosome 21.

claim: Results from dual probe FISH analyses do not support increased trisomy 21 in AD.
source: Thus, results from dual probe FISH analyses do not support increased trisomy 21 in AD but are consistent with alternative CNV mechanisms that could produce APP copy number values exceeding 3, as was observed in 75-genome qPCR analyses (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FISH data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: FISH results are consistent with alternative CNV mechanisms that could produce APP copy number values exceeding 3.
source: Thus, results from dual probe FISH analyses do not support increased trisomy 21 in AD but are consistent with alternative CNV mechanisms that could produce APP copy number values exceeding 3, as was observed in 75-genome qPCR analyses (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an inference based on the FISH and qPCR data.

claim: A total of 154 neuronal nuclei were individually examined from three AD and three non-diseased brains using single-cell qPCR.
source: A total of 154 neuronal nuclei were individually examined from three AD and three non-diseased brains, within which nuclei from the cerebellum and prefrontal cortex were separately analyzed.
evidence: This describes the sample size and experimental design for single-cell qPCR.

claim: In single AD cortical nuclei, significant increases in APP copy number, ranging up to 12 copies in a single nucleus, were observed.
source: In single AD cortical nuclei, significant increases in APP copy number, ranging up to 12 copies in a single nucleus (Figure 6A,B), were observed with a high concordance rate between exons (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A and 6B from single-cell qPCR experiments.

claim: AD cortical nuclei displayed increased average copy numbers (approximately 3.8–4 copies) over control samples (approximately 1.7–2.2 copies).
source: AD cortical nuclei displayed increased average copy numbers (∼3.8–4 copies) over control samples (∼1.7–2.2 copies) (Figure 6A,B), with increased frequencies of high copy number nuclei (six or more copies) (Figures 6C and 5E, red lines) primarily occurring in prefrontal cortex samples (Figure 6C–F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A and 6B from single-cell qPCR experiments.

claim: The AD cortex showed an approximately fourfold increase over the non-diseased cortex of nuclei with greater than 2 APP copies (55–66% vs 12–15%).
source: The AD cortex showed an approximately fourfold increase over the non-diseased cortex of nuclei with greater than 2 APP copies (55–66% vs 12–15%) (Figure 6G,I).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6G and 6I from single-cell qPCR experiments.

claim: In neuronal nuclei with greater than two copies, AD cortical nuclei showed statistically significant increases (approximately 5 copies for both exons) over the other samples (approximately 3 copies for both exons).
source: In addition, nuclei with fewer than 2 APP copies were also identified. In neuronal nuclei with greater than two copies (Figure 6G,I, gold bars), AD cortical nuclei showed statistically significant increases (∼5 copies for both exons) over the other samples (∼3 copies for both exons) (Figure 6H,J).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6H and 6J from single-cell qPCR experiments.

claim: Single-cell qPCR data identify mosaic, neuroanatomically enriched and disease-associated increases in APP copy number in single, sporadic AD neurons.
source: These data identify mosaic, neuroanatomically enriched and disease-associated increases in APP copy number in single, sporadic AD neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the single-cell qPCR data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Nine PNA probes of 12–18 residues, each conjugated to a single Alexa-488 fluor, were designed against multiple sites of the same APP exons examined by single-cell qPCR.
source: Nine PNA probes of 12–18 residues, each conjugated to a single Alexa-488 fluor, were designed against multiple sites of the same APP exons examined by single-cell qPCR, and validated both in silico and by blotting for specificity and linear quantitative behaviors (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This describes the PNA probe design and validation shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Single PNA probes did not produce a detectable signal in any samples using standard fluorescence microscopy.
source: Single PNA probes did not produce a detectable signal in any samples using standard fluorescence microscopy used for aneusomy FISH (Rehen et al., 2001, 2005), contrasting with clearly detectable telomeric signals, which led to evaluation of more sensitive microscopic techniques including confocal, deconvolution (Westra et al., 2010), and ultimately super resolution structured illumination microscopy (N-SIM, Nikon) (Gustafsson, 2000), which all failed to detect possible signals in AD nuclei.
evidence: This describes the technical challenges and optimization process for PNA-FISH detection.

claim: Hybridization of increasing numbers of distinct PNA probes combined with N-SIM visualization resulted in the empirical determination of a threshold that identified one, and rarely two, punctate signals that were much more frequent in AD nuclei.
source: However, hybridization of increasing numbers of distinct PNA probes combined with N-SIM visualization resulted in the empirical determination of a threshold that identified one, and rarely two, punctate signals that were much more frequent in AD nuclei (Figure 7B), and with a frequency consistent with single-cell qPCR data (Figure 6).
evidence: This describes the PNA-FISH methodology and results shown in Figure 7B.

claim: AD neuronal nuclei showed single purely green puncta and rarer two puncta signals.
source: AD neuronal nuclei showed single purely green puncta (Figure 7B, #1 arrow, Video 1–6) and rarer two puncta signals (Figure 7B, #3 arrow, Video 6), all of which could be differentiated from lipofuscin puncta that fluoresced in all channels (Figure 7B, #2 arrow, Video 5).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B and Videos 1-6 from PNA-FISH experiments.

claim: 3D-SIM enabled acquisition and analysis of super resolution projections of individual green puncta revealing a range of morphologies and intensities consistent with varied APP copy number.
source: Use of 3D-SIM enabled acquisition and analysis of super resolution projections of individual green puncta (Figure 7B) revealing a range of morphologies and intensities (Figure 7B,D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1D,E) consistent with varied APP copy number and possibly distinct, intrachromosomal genomic organization.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7B, 7D, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D-E from PNA-FISH experiments.

claim: Threshold detection using multiple PNA probes targeting APP visualized green puncta in 56% of AD neuronal nuclei compared to 22% in non-diseased and 14% in DS.
source: This threshold detection using multiple PNA probes targeting APP visualized green puncta in 56% of AD neuronal nuclei compared to 22% in non-diseased and 14% in DS (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C from PNA-FISH experiments.

claim: There was no evidence of single-copy detection in any sample using PNA-FISH.
source: There was no evidence of single-copy detection in any sample, contrasting with standard FISH data (Figure 5D–I), despite always showing telomeric signals.
evidence: This is an observation from the PNA-FISH experiments indicating the detection threshold.

claim: PNA-FISH fluorescence intensity plots were highly reminiscent of APP copy number plots produced by single-cell qPCR.
source: Compared to single-cell qPCR data, which reports both endogenous alleles in addition to amplification, copy numbers at a single locus below ∼2 were not visualized with PNA-FISH, allowing focused analyses on positive profiles resulting in fluorescence intensity plots ( Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D) that were highly reminiscent of APP copy number plots produced by single-cell qPCR (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a comparison between PNA-FISH data (Figure 7D) and single-cell qPCR data (Figure 6).

claim: The results support a mechanism for the development of sporadic AD whereby the validated familial pathogenic APP gene is mosaically amplified in neurons.
source: Our results support a mechanism for the development of sporadic AD whereby the validated familial pathogenic APP gene is mosaically amplified in neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the multiple lines of experimental evidence presented in the study.

claim: Mosaicism was documented based on multiple independent criteria: increased DCV in 90% of examined AD brains, varied and increased APP copy number in small cohorts, increased APP CNVs in single neurons identified by single-cell qPCR, and APP copy number increases in single nuclei visualized by PNA-FISH.
source: Mosaicism was documented based on multiple independent criteria: increased DCV in 90% of examined AD brains, varied and increased APP copy number in small cohorts, increased APP CNVs in single neurons identified by single-cell qPCR, and APP copy number increases in single nuclei visualized by PNA-FISH.
evidence: This summarizes the multiple lines of experimental evidence presented in the study.

claim: The data are consistent with the inability to substantiate increases in trisomy 21 in cells of the sporadic AD brain.
source: These data are consistent with our inability to substantiate increases in trisomy 21 in cells of the sporadic AD brain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FISH analysis showing no significant increases in trisomy 21.

claim: The concomitant increase in DCV suggests effects on other loci that are also altered in AD.
source: The concomitant increase in DCV suggests effects on other loci that are also altered in AD, the most obvious of which would be copy gains, but which could also involve losses based upon the presence of increased DCV range observed in AD; such loci might contribute to the progeric presentation of sporadic AD and possibly familial forms of AD that still require decades for disease to manifest.
evidence: This is an inference based on the DCV data showing increases beyond what would be expected from APP amplification alone.

claim: The working hypothesis ties the currently accepted pathogenicity of APP gene dosage, established by familial AD and DS, to sporadic AD through a mechanism of somatic, mosaically increased APP copy number in some neurons.
source: Our working hypothesis ties the currently accepted pathogenicity of APP gene dosage, established by familial AD and DS, to sporadic AD through a mechanism of somatic, mosaically increased APP copy number in some neurons.
evidence: This is the central hypothesis of the study based on the experimental findings.

claim: If mosaic genomic changes are downstream of disease onset, APP copy number changes would likely play a significant role in disease progression.
source: Our data do not exclude the possibility that the changes observed are a downstream effect of causative factors in the disease. However, if mosaic genomic changes are downstream of disease onset, APP copy number changes would likely play a significant role in disease progression.
evidence: This is a speculative statement acknowledging alternative interpretations of the data.

claim: Existent single-cell sequencing technology is limited to published sequence resolution between approximately 2-5 Mb and approximately 0.025X genome coverage.
source: However, existent technology is limited to published sequence resolution between ∼2-5 Mb and ∼0.025X genome coverage (Evrony et al., 2012; Gole et al., 2013; McConnell et al., 2013; Cai et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on single-cell sequencing (Evrony et al., 2012; Gole et al., 2013; McConnell et al., 2013; Cai et al., 2014).

claim: Single cell sequencing would be incapable of identifying all but the rarest APP CNVs observed in this study, considering the less than 0.3 Mb size of the APP locus.
source: Considering the <0.3 Mb size of the APP locus, single cell sequencing would be incapable of identifying all but the rarest APP CNVs observed here.
evidence: This is an inference based on the resolution limits of single-cell sequencing and the size of the APP locus.

claim: 320 single, neuronal nuclei were assessed for APP CNVs in this study.
source: While future advances will improve sequence resolution, throughput, and amplification fidelity in single cells, the distinct single cell strategy employed here allowed copy number assessment of a single targeted gene, APP, an approach which may be generalizable to other loci and diseases. Compared to the prior single-neuron reports, 320 single, neuronal nuclei were assessed here for APP CNVs wherein single cell qPCR data markedly resembled PNA-FISH data.
evidence: This describes the sample size for single-cell analyses in the study.

claim: Single cell qPCR data markedly resembled PNA-FISH data.
source: Compared to the prior single-neuron reports, 320 single, neuronal nuclei were assessed here for APP CNVs wherein single cell qPCR data markedly resembled PNA-FISH data.
evidence: This is a comparison of the two independent single-cell methods used in the study.

claim: The use of PNA-FISH does not require any amplification or normalization.
source: The use of PNA-FISH does not require any amplification or normalization, and yet PNA-FISH and single-cell qPCR produced a highly similar distribution of APP copy number amplifications.
evidence: This describes a methodological advantage of PNA-FISH over other techniques.

claim: PNA-FISH and single-cell qPCR produced a highly similar distribution of APP copy number amplifications.
source: The use of PNA-FISH does not require any amplification or normalization, and yet PNA-FISH and single-cell qPCR produced a highly similar distribution of APP copy number amplifications.
evidence: This is a comparison of results from the two independent methods.

claim: The employed techniques were not capable of assessing intact neurons or their histological organization.
source: The employed techniques were not capable of assessing intact neurons or their histological organization, which will require technological modifications.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the current methodology.

claim: At this time the precise structure of APP CNVs and the mechanisms leading to their existence are unknown.
source: Finally, these techniques are currently capable of interrogating only parts of the entire APP locus; therefore, at this time the precise structure of APP CNVs and the mechanisms leading to their existence are unknown.
evidence: This acknowledges limitations in understanding the detailed structure and mechanisms of APP CNVs.

claim: The prevailing amyloid hypothesis in AD posits that Aβ deposition drives AD.
source: First, the prevailing amyloid hypothesis in AD posits that Aβ deposition drives AD (Hardy and Selkoe, 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Hardy and Selkoe, 2002.

claim: Increased incidences of amyloid senile plaques are observed in all forms of AD and appear to be directly linked to APP dosage in DS and familial AD.
source: Increased incidences of amyloid senile plaques are observed in all forms of AD and appear to be directly linked to APP dosage in DS and familial AD.
evidence: This is established knowledge based on prior research on AD, DS, and familial AD.

claim: The mosaic increases in neuronal APP copy number provide an explanation for the universal presence of Aβ senile plaques in sporadic forms of AD despite an absence of constitutive copy number gain.
source: The mosaic increases in neuronal APP copy number reported here provide an explanation for the universal presence of Aβ senile plaques in sporadic forms—indeed, all forms—of AD despite an absence of constitutive copy number gain.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the study's findings to the amyloid hypothesis.

claim: The presence of rare neurons with APP amplifications in non-diseased brains provides an explanation for the observed presence of senile plaques in otherwise normal, aged brains.
source: The presence of rare neurons with APP amplifications in non-diseased brains also provides an explanation for the observed presence of senile plaques in otherwise normal, aged brains (Gibson, 1983; Cras et al., 1991; Mackenzie et al., 1996), consistent with the ages of non-diseased brains examined here, which exceeded 75 years.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the study's findings to prior observations of plaques in aged brains, supported by citations (Gibson, 1983; Cras et al., 1991; Mackenzie et al., 1996).

claim: APP amplification in AD is consistent with dysregulation of normally occurring processes in the etiology of AD pathogenesis.
source: Along with the occurrence and augmentation of DCV, APP amplification in AD is consistent with dysregulation of normally occurring processes in the etiology of AD pathogenesis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of APP amplification in both AD and non-diseased brains, but at different frequencies.

claim: The lack of observed increases of trisomy 21 in sporadic AD are consistent with prior studies in both peripheral non-brain and intact brain tissues, which reported APP levels approximating 2N.
source: Moreover, the lack of observed increases of trisomy 21 in sporadic AD are consistent with prior studies in both peripheral non-brain and intact brain tissues, which reported APP levels approximating 2N (Podlisny et al., 1987; St George-Hyslop et al., 1987; Tanzi et al., 1987; Bertram et al., 2010), and is further consistent with mosaic CNVs observed here.
evidence: This connects the study's findings to prior literature, supported by citations (Podlisny et al., 1987; St George-Hyslop et al., 1987; Tanzi et al., 1987; Bertram et al., 2010).

claim: The results do not eliminate roles for mosaic aneuploidy in AD, but do not support trisomy 21 as a specific mechanism for increasing APP copy number in sporadic AD.
source: Our results do not eliminate roles for mosaic aneuploidy in AD, but do not support trisomy 21 as a specific mechanism for increasing APP copy number in sporadic AD.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FISH analysis data.

claim: DCV analyses detected maximum gains of approximately 21% and average gains of approximately 8.2% over lymphocytes.
source: Our DCV analyses detected maximum gains of ∼21% and average gains of ∼8.2% over lymphocytes, representing a fraction of the 100% increase expected in a 4N cell.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the DNA content analysis.

claim: The subgenomic increases observed are consistent with the reported absence of adult neurogenesis in the normal cerebral cortex.
source: The subgenomic increases observed here are also consistent with the reported absence of adult neurogenesis in the normal cerebral cortex (Rakic, 2002; Bhardwaj et al., 2006), and could also be relevant to reports of nucleotide incorporation in adult cortical neurons (Gould et al., 1999).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the study's findings to prior literature on neurogenesis, supported by citations (Rakic, 2002; Bhardwaj et al., 2006; Gould et al., 1999).

claim: Concepts involving changes in DNA synthesis in AD without cell-cycle progression or neurogenesis could be rectified through subgenomic DNA synthesis in post-mitotic neurons.
source: Concepts involving changes in DNA synthesis in AD without cell-cycle progression or neurogenesis could be rectified through subgenomic DNA synthesis in post-mitotic neurons that might involve DNA synthetic proteins reported in AD (Copani et al., 2002, 2006).
evidence: This is a speculative statement connecting the study's findings to prior reports of DNA synthesis in AD, supported by citations (Copani et al., 2002, 2006).

claim: The observed genomic alterations in AD could occur through both developmental as well as aging processes.
source: The observed genomic alterations in AD could occur through both developmental as well as aging processes as reported for at least one form of mosaicism, aneuploidies (Bushman and Chun, 2013) that have been linked to caspase-mediated cell death (Peterson et al., 2012) and could have relevance to developmental APP functions (Nikolaev et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the timing of genomic alterations, supported by citations (Bushman and Chun, 2013; Peterson et al., 2012; Nikolaev et al., 2009).

claim: Developmental cell death processes involve DNA fragmentation and double strand breaks.
source: Perhaps tellingly, these developmental cell death processes also involve DNA fragmentation and double strand breaks (Blaschke et al., 1996; Staley et al., 1997; Blaschke et al., 1998) that have recently been reported in neurons exposed to physiological and AD stimuli (Suberbielle et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Blaschke et al., 1996; Staley et al., 1997; Blaschke et al., 1998; Suberbielle et al., 2013).

claim: It is possible that somatic mosaicism may arise through dysfunction of normally operative DNA repair mechanisms that produce DCV in the normal brain, with augmentation in the diseased brain.
source: It is possible that somatic mosaicism may arise through dysfunction of normally operative DNA repair mechanisms that produce DCV in the normal brain, with augmentation in the diseased brain.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanisms underlying somatic mosaicism.

claim: Increased DCV and APP CNVs observed in AD may in part reflect neurons that have delayed or averted cell death, wherein somatic genomic changes could provide a survival advantage at a cost of altered neurophysiological functions.
source: We speculate that increased DCV and APP CNVs observed in AD may in part reflect neurons that have delayed or averted cell death, wherein somatic genomic changes could provide a survival advantage at a cost of altered neurophysiological functions.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the functional consequences of genomic mosaicism.

claim: The DNA content changes observed showed not only disease relationships but also varied with brain region and cell type.
source: The DNA content changes observed here showed not only disease relationships but also varied with brain region and cell type.
evidence: This is a summary of the DNA content analysis findings showing regional and cell-type specificity.

claim: The interrogated neurons are likely terminal in their fate: they will not divide further.
source: It is important to note that the interrogated neurons are likely terminal in their fate: they will not divide further, contrasting with lymphocytes that, perhaps surprisingly, showed the least amount of DCV despite being a proliferating population.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about neuronal post-mitotic state.

claim: Lymphocytes showed the least amount of DCV despite being a proliferating population.
source: It is important to note that the interrogated neurons are likely terminal in their fate: they will not divide further, contrasting with lymphocytes that, perhaps surprisingly, showed the least amount of DCV despite being a proliferating population.
evidence: This is an observation from the DNA content analysis comparing neurons to lymphocytes.

claim: Proliferating lymphocytes may be similar to stem and progenitor populations that can maintain germline genomes to promote population expansion.
source: Unlike neurons, proliferating lymphocytes may be similar to stem and progenitor populations that can maintain germline genomes to promote population expansion.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about why lymphocytes show less DCV.

claim: Many dividing cells that deviate significantly from the germline genome would be incapable of further division and are eliminated by cell death.
source: By contrast, neurons are by definition post-mitotic, and therefore not subject to this possible requirement. We think it likely that many dividing cells that deviate significantly from the germline genome—and thus would be incapable of further division—are eliminated by cell death and would be removed from the population interrogated for DNA content.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about selection against genomic variation in dividing cells.

claim: The most extremely aneuploid forms of neuroprogenitor cells appear to be eliminated by caspase-mediated cell death.
source: Support for this view includes reports on aneuploidies in neuroprogenitor cells, whereby the most extremely aneuploid forms appear to be eliminated by caspase-mediated cell death (Blaschke et al., 1996, 1998; Peterson et al., 2011; Peterson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Blaschke et al., 1996, 1998; Peterson et al., 2011; Peterson et al., 2012).

claim: DNA content changes may be contextual, enabling diverse functions in different cell types.
source: DNA content changes may therefore be contextual, enabling diverse functions in different cell types.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the functional significance of DCV.

claim: The large differences observed even between brain regions and amongst neuronal nuclei would suggest the existence of distinct neuronal functions produced by DCV.
source: The large differences observed even between brain regions and amongst neuronal nuclei would suggest the existence of distinct neuronal functions produced by DCV, and possibly specific processes or stimuli that can genomically alter neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the regional and cell-to-cell variability in DCV.

claim: Diverse stimuli previously implicated as AD risk factors including age and trauma might share common endpoints via influences on genomic mosaicism.
source: Diverse stimuli previously implicated as AD risk factors including age and trauma (Sparks et al., 1990; Plassman et al., 2000), might share common endpoints via influences on genomic mosaicism.
evidence: This is a speculative statement connecting AD risk factors to genomic mosaicism, supported by citations (Sparks et al., 1990; Plassman et al., 2000).

claim: The consequences of somatic APP amplification in AD may support functionality of other somatically altered genomic loci observed in single neurons that could contribute to the progeric presentation of AD as well as aspects of the disease itself.
source: The consequences of somatic APP amplification in AD may support functionality of other somatically altered genomic loci observed in single neurons that could contribute to the progeric presentation of AD as well as aspects of the disease itself.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader implications of genomic mosaicism in AD.

claim: Other sporadic or idiopathic brain diseases could arise through altered genomic mosaicism that includes somatic variations at both known and unknown pathogenic loci.
source: We further hypothesize that other sporadic or idiopathic brain diseases could arise through altered genomic mosaicism that includes somatic variations at both known and unknown pathogenic loci.
evidence: This is a speculative statement extending the findings to other brain diseases.
